questions.question: What three files form the smallest useful workbench?
options: README.md for onboarding, CHANGELOG.md for history, and LICENSE for legal terms
model.py for the model client, prompts.py for templates, and tools.py for function defs
Dockerfile for the build, Makefile for commands, and .gitignore for excluded paths
AGENTS.md (router), agent_state.json (state), task_board.json (queue)
questions.explanation: A short router, durable state, and a task queue are the floor.

questions.question: What is the lesson's framing of AGENTS.md?
options: A short router that points at deeper docs and the state and board
A 3000-line onboarding manual covering every edge case the agent could hit
A pure prompt-cache key used only to reduce token cost on repeated calls
A secret kept out of the repo and injected only at deployment time
questions.explanation: AGENTS.md is a router, not a manual; long manuals get ignored.

questions.question: What does Augment Code's data say about a good AGENTS.md?
options: It has no measurable effect on task success once the underlying model is already capable enough for the task
A good AGENTS.md gives a quality jump equivalent to upgrading from Haiku to Opus; a bad one is worse than no file
Length always helps; the longer and more exhaustive the AGENTS.md file, the better the agent performs on every task
Only Claude reads it; other coding agents like Codex, Cursor, and Copilot ignore the file entirely
questions.explanation: Augment Code's measurement: best files are model-upgrade-shaped, worst are worse than nothing.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend file-backed state over chat-history state?
options: Disk is cheaper than paying for extra context tokens on every single model call inside the agent loop
Files are smaller than the equivalent chat transcript once compressed with gzip
Chat history is volatile; the file survives session death, conversation trimming, and tool resets
It is required by SOC 2 compliance audits for every production agent deployment
questions.explanation: Sessions die and chat gets trimmed; the file is the durable system of record.

questions.question: What does the lesson say happens when conflicting instructions land in AGENTS.md?
options: Latency drops
Conflicting instructions silently drop the agent from interactive to greedy mode (AMBIG-SWE: 48.8% to 28% resolve rate)
Cost rises slightly
Nothing
questions.explanation: AMBIG-SWE measured a large resolve-rate drop when contradictions appear; number priorities instead.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend cross-tool symlinks like CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md?
options: So a single source of truth fans out to every coding agent without forking
To save bytes by avoiding duplicate copies of the same instructions across tool directories
To pass auditing requirements that mandate a single canonical instructions file per repo
To satisfy the MIT license terms attached to the agents.md open specification
questions.explanation: Symlinks (or Nx-style generators) keep one canonical source across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, etc.
